title: [BUG] Instruction fetch misaligned exception raised when a conditional branch that is not taken
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hi,

According to the RISC-V 2.2 specification p.11: 
> An instruction address misaligned exception is generated on a taken branch or unconditional jump if the target address is not four-byte aligned. **No instruction fetch misaligned exception is generated for a conditional branch that is not taken**

But in `core/branch_unit.sv`, the exception is raised in branch unit as long as target address is misaligned *without taking the conditional branch result into account* :
`if (branch_valid_i && target_address[0] != 1'b0) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;` from [line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/72143ef0a9b50f2aaffa708a55263a5971bf0354/core/branch_unit.sv#L94) 

The fix should augment the `if` condition to include condition check that validate it is either an unconditional jump  or a **taken** conditional branch.


Thanks!

title: [Possible Issue] Non-selectable address matching mode leads to an incorrect PMP configuration update
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Instruction execution field `X`, and probably others, of PMP configuration CSRs is not updated correctly when trying to write non-selectable address matching value of field `A` in case PMP granularity `G` is `1`. Is this intended?

### RISC-V Specification
Unprivileged ISA: [20191213](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1s0lZxUZaa7eV_O0_WsZzaurFLLww7ou5/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20211203](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EMip5dZlnypTk7pt4WWUKmtjUKTOkBqh/view) | External Debug Support: [0.13.02](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XSPqW3WIfflIMeuGJBxGTMOEyeuRAQ5F/view)
> The PMP configuration registers are densely packed into CSRs to minimize context-switch time.
For RV32, sixteen CSRs, pmpcfg0–pmpcfg15, hold the configurations pmp0cfg–pmp63cfg for the 64
PMP entries, as shown in Figure 3.31.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/09e7e476-c3a1-40c0-8a69-e2a59804d6f5)

> Figure 3.35 shows the layout of a PMP configuration register. The R, W, and X bits, when set,
indicate that the PMP entry permits read, write, and instruction execution, respectively. When
one of these bits is clear, the corresponding access type is denied. The R, W, and X fields form a
collectiveWARL field for which the combinations with R=0 and W=1 are reserved. The remaining
two fields, A and L, are described in the following sections.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/ca0ef0fb-261a-4e5d-a7ca-577121aa18ac)

> The A field in a PMP entry’s configuration register encodes the address-matching mode of the
associated PMP address register.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/ec536bae-9b3f-4c48-90d4-4b555cf78c8e)

> Although the PMP mechanism supports regions as small as four bytes, platforms may specify
coarser PMP regions. In general, the PMP grain is 2G+2 bytes and must be the same across all
PMP regions. When G ≥ 1, the NA4 mode is not selectable.


### Example Scenario

As shown below, the following sequence of instructions happens: 
> CSRRS x0, pmp_cfg0, x1

The instruction `CSRRS x0, pmp_cfg0, x1` is decoded at `t_id` and executed in machine mode resulting in updating the architecture state at `t_arch_update`. As a result, instruction execution field `X` of `pmp3cfg` is not updated as expected. Where it's supposed to be set according to the written value of `x1`. Probably the reason for that is trying to write `NA4` value to the `A` field of the same register `pmp3cfg`, which is not selectable when the granularity `G` is `1`, and thus updating `A` is ignored correctly, but `X` has to be updated correctly still!

![Issue_15](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/872e3b2d-8c2d-4e2e-a45c-f111867ef021)

### Steps to Reproduce

Git Hash: [de2e254c](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/de2e254cd4c2d3e3a6d4def1652918e8f2535512) | TARGET_CFG: [cv32a6_imac_sv0](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/include/cv32a6_imac_sv0_config_pkg.sv) | VCD: [issue_15.zip](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/files/14836579/issue_15.zip)

### Component
**Component:RTL**

---
Product: Questa OneSpin Solutions
App: Questa Processor App
Tool's version: 2024.1_1

title: [BUG] Wrong exception cause being raised in CSR Logic (illegal instruction instead of Virtual Instruction exception)
[BUG] An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6
body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found an efficient and fault-tolerant Meltdown vulnerability on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data at arbitrary addresses from user space. This vulnerability takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit. Thus, we can access privilege data in a transient execution window and encode the privileged data in the microarchitecture. We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ```asm 2f40: fdiv.d fa5,fa5,fa4 2f44: lb t1, 0(a0) # a0 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe06f30, secret data is 0x30 2f48: slli t1, t1, 5 # encode secret to a probe array (index = secret << 5, t1 = 0x30 << 5 = 0x600) 2f4c: add t0, t1, t0 # encode secret to a probe array (base = 0x10000, t0 = base + t1 = 0x10600) 2f50: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode the secret to cache ``` The code runs under U-mode. The `lb` at `0x2f44` tries to access `0xffffffffffe06f30`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of `fdiv` and the function [unit ready status](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L413), subsequent instructions will be issued during the `fdiv` transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the commit signals, **G2** represents scoreboard entries and **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of` ld` at `0x2f50`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. In fact, when executing the `lb` at `0x2f44` architecturally, a load page fault exception will be triggered, and `t1` result will be 0. However, this is not important. We have already encoded the secret in the microarchitecture. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x105e0`, `0x10600`, `0x10620`, and `0x10640`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ```asm probe: li t0, 0x10600 2f7c: ld t1, -32(t0) # cache miss 2f80: ld t1, 0(t0) # cache hit, addr = 0x10000 + 0x30 << 5 2f84: ld t1, 32(t0) # cache miss 2f88: ld t1, 64(t0) # cache miss ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10600`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. It is worth noting that this vulnerability has a high level of **fault tolerance**. Even if the secret address results in a TLB miss, this transient window is long enough to complete the Page Table Walk process. Similarly, if the address of the probe array also results in a TLB miss, the Page Table Walk can still be completed, and the secret can be encoded in the TLB. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. [rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24147141/rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip)

title: [BUG] Out-of-Order Not Working
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

## Bug Explanation

I noticed the docs say that Out-of-Order can occur between the multiplier and the ALU, however this is not the case according to the RTL.

Docs:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/a29b231070f2dccca53eae2681120116633a4ffc/docs/03_cva6_design/issue_stage.md?plain=1#L42-L54

RTL:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/adf99b53042d2b14cbbb36689babf8cd4c03cf81/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L135-L152

For example, I have this code snippet:

```
        div     t2, t0, t1
        fsqrt.s f1, f1
        lw      t5, 0(s1)
        add     t6, t0, t1
```

And this is it's execute stage:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43790149/223483191-73f6885e-c1e1-4930-bf28-4377288d72b6.png)

As you can see, the `add` instruction isn't run until after the `div` finishes.

## Proposed Fix

Either:

* The RTL could be changed to separate the ALU and multiplier into two separate busy signals.
* The example in the docs could be changed to something else, such as `div` and `lsu`.

comments.body: If you like, I can submit a pull request changing the docs to give div and lsu as the example

Hello @sifferman and thanks for opening this issue.

I had a look, I think I have found a too strict restriction (#1230) related to `mult -> *` sequences. However it does not seem to fix this issue about `div -> flu` sequences.

The parallelism is only possible for units spread on different result buses, so that their result can be provided to the scoreboard without conflicts. For the `div -> add` sequence you show, they use the same result bus (named `flu` as "fixed latency unit", even if div does not have a fixed latency), so you are right, the doc example is wrong.

A few suggestions/ideas:

- We can update the docs as you suggest.
- We could add a write-back port for `mult/div` but we won't as the area cost would be considerable!
- We can check if there is a minimal latency for div; if so, maybe we could issue a few other FLU instructions just after the `div` starts?
- Maybe we could modify how the div result is handled: when div result is available, if result bus is available then push the result, else store it in a (new?) register and lock the `flu` issues until the result bus is available, then release the lock and push the result.
- Maybe we could move the `mult/div` unit to the same port as FP operations?

Thanks for taking a look @cathales! I agree with your observations.

Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

I will have time to look into it in about a month if progress hasn't been made on it sooner

If we move mult/div to FP port, I hope multiply-accumulate would not need bubbles anymore if the compiler is smart enough to avoid RAW hasards like below:

```asm
mul m0, a, b
; begin repeat
mul m1, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m0 ; now: bubble because same bus than previous mul -> after modification: issue ok
mul m0, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m1 ; bubble -> issue ok
; end repeat
add r, r, m0 ; issue ok
```

However, if the compiler does not do that (see below), there will be the same bubbles anyway so the modification will not impact performance.

```asm
; begin repeat
mul m, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m ; bubble because needs m from mul above and mul duration is 2 cycles
; end repeat
````

> Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

For CoreMark the increase would be less than 3%, but it depends of the application.

About area:

For a configuration with both F and M, we use an existing write-back port so it is okay.

For a configuration with M, without F, today there should not be a write-back port for FPU, so the muxes in the scoreboard could be cheap. If we add one port for the multiplier, it means that the muxes are big.

So maybe the performance vs area cost should be discussed.

title: [BUG] About four-byte alignment on target addresses of control transfer instructions (branch_unit.sv)
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hi,
 
In `core/branch_unit.sv` the `branch_exception_o.valid` is raised high only if the branch/jump target address is not aligned **on a two-byte boundary** ([line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/513bb91f823a18a6653a1685acd60408049c9c8f/core/branch_unit.sv#L94C8-L96C10) checks only the LSB). That is, it enforces only two-byte boundary check, and does not raise exception when target address of JAL/JALR is not four-byte aligned. 
However, in RISC-V 2.1 specification p.16 says "The JAL and JALR instructions can generate a misaligned instruction fetch exception if the target address is not aligned to a four-byte boundary."

If my understanding is correct, I think the fix may need to change the condition of [line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/513bb91f823a18a6653a1685acd60408049c9c8f/core/branch_unit.sv#L94C8-L96C10) from. 
`if (branch_valid_i && target_address[0] != 1'b0) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;` to   
`if (branch_valid_i && (target_address[1:0] != 2'b00)) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;`

Thanks!

comments.body:
Hello @Bill94l, thank you for reporting the issue.

I will take a look on it, and let you know.

As you can see, the write-back mode of the HPDcache is not yet officially supported on the CVA6 as there is no a corresponding configuration, so you may have some issues. But anyway, It should in principle work.

Ok, I diagnosed the issue but I did not yet fixed it. It is not a very simple one. It is an integration bug: hpdcache in WB mode within the CVA6.

It is a cache coherency issue between the Icache and the Dcache (HPDcache). The runtime in the v-tests (tests with virtual memory), modifies instruction segments. These modifications are done locally in the HPDcache (because of the write-back mode), and are not visible by the instruction cache unless the HPDcache is flushed (this is not required when in write-through mode because the memory is always updated on writes). The runtime explicitly does this using a fence.i instruction, but currently this instruction only requests an invalidation of the Icache with no flush of the Dcache.

I need to modify the CVA6 controller to issue a CMO flush operation to the HPDCache in case of a fence.i instruction, or find another clever way to keep both caches coherent... I have some ideas but I will think it over a little more.

You will need to be a little patient for this one.

Hi @Bill94l,

The fix is on its way. I have an opened Pull Request #2691 that fixes the coherency issue between the Icache and the Dcache when using the HPDcache in WB mode.

title: [BUG] Spectre-type Vulnerability and Its Different Variants were Found in CVA6
body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ## Summary We creatively used `ecall` to delay the resolution of the branch, creating a branch misprediction transient window. In this window, we can access kernel-space data and encode it in different microarchitecture components at U-mode without exception. ## Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found Spectre vulnerability and its different variants on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data from user space without exception. CVA6 employs thie Scoreboard for out-of-order issuing. The Scoreboard algorithm won't issue instructions that have RAW conflicts. Therefore, when a B-type instruction is issued, its operands are already ready. So, B-type instructions can be resolved very quickly. As a result, the traditional Spectre vulnerabilities cannot perform the secret access and encoding operation within the CVA6's 1-2 cycles branch midprediction window. However, we creatively introduce `ecall` to delay the resolution of the branch. `ecall` is a instruction that will implicitly write register `a0`. But in the implementation of CVA6 Scoreboard, `ecall` won't be in conflict with the subsequent instructions that take `a0` as an operand. This give us a chance to issue B-type instruction with operand `a0`. CVA6 will read the old value of `a0` and make a wrong descision on the B-type instrucion. Then, we accessed and encoded the secret on the wrong branch. This takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 Scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit, which we have illustrated in detail in previous issue: [An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/3163). We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall # overwrite a0 to a non-zero value 2f48: bnez a0, 2f84 # the old value of a0 is zero 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe04000 2f50: slli t0, t0, 0x5 # use secret as index 2f54: add t0, t1, t0 # t1 contains probe array address 0x10000 2f58: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode secret to probe array ... 2f84 : # the true control flow will jump to here ... ``` The code runs under U-mode. `a0` is initialized to 0. The `lb` at `0x2f4c` tries to access `0xffffffffffe04000`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of fdiv and the misprediction of `bnez`, subsequent instructions will be issued during the transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the [commit signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/scoreboard.sv#L100).**G2** represents [Scoreboard entries](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/scoreboard.sv#L100). **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors, including [`lsu_valid_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L52), [`vaddr_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L575), [`paddr_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L579), [`miss_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/wt_dcache.sv#L37), [`mem_rtrn_vld_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/wt_dcache.sv#L51), `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`, `io_axi4_0_ar_bits_addr` and `io_axi4_0_r_valid`. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the Scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of `ld` at `0x2f58`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. After `ecall` trap process finished, `a0` will be modified to a non-zero value. `bnez` at `0x2f48` will taken and control flow will skip these instructions between `0x2f4c` and `0x2f58`. But these instructions have been microarchitecturally executed. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x10000`, `0x10010`, `0x10020`, and `0x10030`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ``` 5000: lui t0, 0x10 5004: ld t1, 0(t0) # t0 = 0x10000 5008: ld t1, 16(t0) 500c: ld t1, 32(t0) 5010: ld t1, 48(t0) ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10020`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit [aa4f5a5](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd) and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. ## Variants In CVA6, not only the DCache can be used as a component for encoding and decoding secrets. We have discovered that the frontend states, such as BTB, BHT, RAS, etc., can be changed within the transient window. And after the speculation execution was rolled back, these states will not be rolled back. Thus, secrets can be encoded in these front-end components. ### BTB [BTB](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L28) is a frontend branch prediction unit. It provides branch prediction for `jalr` instructions except for `call` and `ret`. BTB will record the target addresses of these `jalr` instructions, and when it encounters the corresponding `jalr` again in the future, it will directly predict the jump address to be the recorded target address. As shown in the following code, we have constructed a jump address that depends on the secret. Depending on the secret, the target address for the `jalr` instruction located at `0x2f58` will change. During the transient window, after the `jalr` target jump address is calculated, the BTB entries will be updated. After the transient window rollback, the BTB entries will not be invalidated, so we will keep the secret in the BTB. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 80002f9c 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: slli t0, t0, 0x2 2f54: add t1, t1, t0 # t1 contains probe address 2f58 : 2f58: jalr t0, t1 # train the btb, different secret will reseult in different target address ... 2f8c : 2f8c: nop 2f90: nop 2f94: nop 2f98: nop ... ``` As shown in the following two waveform figures. We changed the value of secret and ran the testcase. When the secret is 0, the predicted jump address of the corresponding entry in the BTB will be updated to `2f8c`. When the secret is 1, the predicted jump address of the corresponding entry in the BTB will be updated to `2f90`. **G5** represents [BTB update signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L45). **secret = 0** **secret != 0** Next, we will attempt to decode the data. Based on the analysis of the [BTB entry matching mechanism](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L69), we found that BTB makes predictions only based on the lower bits of the PC, and does not match the entire PC. Therefore, we use the following instruction for decoding. ``` 5000: la t1, probe # t1 = 0x2f8c ... 5058: jalr t0, t1 ``` During the decoding stage, we placed a `jalr` instruction at the address `0x5058`. This address shares the same BTB entry with the `jalr` instruction that previously encoded the secret at `0x2f58`. So it will trigger branch prediction. **G4** represents [BTB prediction signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L47). If the secret is 0, then the branch prediction is correct and the execution time is shorter. If the secret is 1, then the branch prediction is incorrect and the execution time will be slower. So this creates a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### BHT [BHT](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv) is also a frontend branch predictor. It records the jump situations of the B-type instructions. When it encounters the corresponding B-type instructions again, it makes branch prediction based on the recorded historical information. This BHT uses a 2-bit [saturation counter](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L56) to record the historical taken/untaken situations. If a B-type instruction is taken, the saturation counter of the corresponding entry is incremented by one. When the value of the saturation counter is greater than or equal to 2, it predicts that the B-type instruction will be taken in the future. We conduct the following testcase. The `beqz` instruction at `0x2f50` is taken/untaken based on whether the secret is zero. We use this instruction to encode the secret. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2f80 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: 2f50: beqz t0, 2f7c # train BHT ... 2f7c : ``` The two waveform diagrams below illustrate the encoding stages under different secrets. **G5** represents the [BHT entry](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L59) corresponding to the `beqz` instruction. When the secret is 0, the `beqz` instruction is taken and updates the corresponding saturation counter to 1. When the secret is 1, the `beqz` instruction is untaken, and the saturation counter for the corresponding entry remains unchanged and stays at 0. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We use the following instructions to decode the secret. Similar to BTB, BHT also only matches the lower bits of the PC to determine a BHT entry. We placed a `beqz` instruction at the address `0x5050`. This instruction will use the same BHT entry as the `beqz` instruction that encodes secret at address `0x2f50`. We set `t0` to 0 so that the `beqz` instruction will be taken. Then we observe the behavior of the `beqz` instruction at address 0x5050 at its second time execution. ``` 5000: li t0, 0 ... 5050: beqz t0, 5000 ``` **G4** represents the [BHT prediction result](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L42) for the `beqz` instruction at address `0x5050`. When the secret is 0, this BHT entry records two branch takens. Therefore, when the instruction at `0x5050` is executed for the second time, the BHT will predicte it to be taken. The branch prediction is correct and the execution time is faster. When the secret is 1, this BHT entry records only one branch taken. The BHT will predicte it to be untaken. The branch prediction is incorrect and the execution time slows down. This forms a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### RAS [RAS](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv) is used to push the return address onto the stack when making a call. We attempted to utilize RAS to create a temporal side-channel. By performing secret-dependent RAS operations within the transient window, the secret is encoded within the RAS. After the transient window rollback, the status of RAS will not be revoked. This enables the decoding of the secret. In the following testcase, `ra` is influenced by the secret. If the secret is 0, then the `jalr` instruction located at `0x2f58` will be executed. Executing this instruction will push the address of the next instruction into RAS, thereby changing the state of RAS. If the secret is not zero, then `0x2f58` will be skipped and the state of RAS will not be changed. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5,fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2fb0 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: add ra, t2, t0 # t2 is initialized to 0x2f58. RAS top = previous call address + 4 2f54: ret # pop RAS. if t0 == 0, continue to execute 0x2f58 2f58: jalr ra, t3 # push 0x2f5c into RAS. RAS top = 0x2f5c ``` **G4** represents the RAS-related signal. Including the push signal [`push_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L29), the data pushed onto the stack [`data_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L33), the pop signal [`pop_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L31), the valid signal indicating the availability of the top stack data [`data_o.valid`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L35), and the data at the top of the stack [`data_o.ra`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L35). When the secret is 0, the `jalr` instruction at `0x2f58` within the transient window is executed, pushing `0x2f5c` into the stack. When the secret is not 0, the state of RAS has not changed. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We use the following code to decode the secret. We execute an instruction that returns to `0x2f5c`. At this point, RAS is used for target address prediction. This address is precisely the value that was pushed into RAS when the secret was 0. ``` 5000: li ra, 0x2f5c 5008: ret ``` Observe the ret instruction located at 0x5008. If the value of "secret" is 0, the prediction is correct and the execution time is fast. If the value of "secret" is not 0, the prediction will be incorrect and the execution time will be slow. This forms a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### ICache All the instructions executed by CVA6 come from the [ICache](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv). The reading of instructions is strongly related to the control flow. So we attempted to influence the control flow through "secret", thereby affecting the state of the ICache, in order to encode the secret into the ICache. In the following testcase, a secret-dependent `beqz` instruction was placed at the address `0x2f50`. If the secret is 0, it will jump to the `probe` instruction block. It is necessary to ensure beforehand that the `probe` instruction block is not in the ICache. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2f90 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) 2f50: beqz t0, 2f80 ... 2f80 : ``` **G4** represents the signals related to the ICache, including the ICache miss signal [`miss_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv#L50) and the instructions request signal [`areq_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv#L52). When the secret is 0, the control flow needs to jump to the `probe` instruction block at address `0x2f80`. Since the `probe` instruction is not located in the ICache, an ICache miss occurred. At this point, the ICache initiates a refill request to the memory. Ultimately, the content of the `probe` instruction block is filled back into the ICache. However, when the secret is not zero, the `probe` instruction block will not be filled into the ICache. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We directly execute the probe instruction block and observe the execution time. ``` 5000: j 2f80 ``` It can be observed that when the secret is 0, the `probe` instruction block has already been loaded into the ICache during the transient window, so when jumping to the `probe` instruction block, it can be executed directly. However, when the secret is not zero, the `probe` instruction block will not be loaded in the transient window. Thus, an ICache miss occurs and the instruction needs to be fetched from the memory, resulting in a significant time difference. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ## Conclusion Overall, although CVA6 uses the scoreboard for instruction scheduling and inherently has a relatively small transient execution window, it can still be bypassed in various ways. Moreover, the microarchitecture of CVA6 has numerous timing vulnerabilities. title: [BUG] Access faults report physical address in tval
body:
I noticed that the PMP exception reporting in CVA6 returns the physical address as exception `tval`, e.g., [here](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/mmu_sv39/mmu.sv#L369C25-L369C41) and [here](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/mmu_sv39/mmu.sv#L379), where `lsu_paddr_o` is the address the PMP checks are performed against, i.e., [here](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/mmu_sv39/mmu.sv#L436), so it must be the final translated physical address.

This is explicitly against the privileged spec: 


> 3.1.16 Machine Trap Value Register (mtval):
> If mtval is written with a nonzero value when a breakpoint, address-misaligned, access-fault, or
page-fault exception occurs on an instruction fetch, load, or store, then mtval will contain the
faulting virtual address.
> When page-based virtual memory is enabled, mtval is written with the faulting virtual address,
even for physical-memory access-fault exceptions.
>  
>  4.1.9 Supervisor Trap Value (stval) Register:
> If stval is written with a nonzero value when a breakpoint, address-misaligned, access-fault, or
page-fault exception occurs on an instruction fetch, load, or store, then stval will contain the
faulting virtual address.

Is there a reason behind this choice or is it just a latent bug?

title: [BUG] Incorrect Setting of DZ Flag for 0/0 Division
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

I have observed an incorrect behavior in the CVA6 core regarding the handling of the 0/0 division operation. Specifically, the Divide by Zero (`DZ`) flag is incorrectly set for this operation, which according to IEEE 754 standards (Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic section 7.3):

>7.3 Division by zero 7.3.0 
The divideByZero exception shall be signaled if and only if an exact infinite result is defined for an  operation on finite operands. The default result of divideByZero shall be an ∞ correctly signed according to the operation:
― For division, when the divisor is zero and the dividend is a finite non-zero number, the sign of the infinity is the exclusive OR of the operands’ signs (see 6.3).

So, it should only trigger the Invalid Operation (`NV`) flag, since 0/0 is an undefined operation resulting in NaN.

**The log is as follows:**
```
core   0: 0x0000000080005aa0 (0x001025f3) csrrs   a1, fflags, zero
1 0x0000000080005aa0 (0x001025f3) x11 0x0000000000000000
core   0: 0x0000000080005aa4 (0x221080d3) fsgnj.d ft1, ft1, ft1
1 0x0000000080005aa4 (0x221080d3) f 1 0x0000000000000000
core   0: 0x0000000080005aa8 (0x1a10f953) fdiv.d  fs2, ft1, ft1
1 0x0000000080005aa8 (0x1a10f953) f18 0x7ff8000000000000
core   0: 0x0000000080005aac (0x00102673) csrrs   a2, fflags, zero
1 0x0000000080005aac (0x00102673) x12 0x0000000000000018
```

I agree with you — in the case of a misaligned exception, we should avoid sending a lookup request to the TLB.

```

body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Some 16 bits illegal instructions (because of a specific bit) can be decoded as C.sh, which is part of the Zcb extension. ## RISC-V Specification Unprivileged ISA: [20250508](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1uviu1nH-tScFfgrovvFCrj7Omv8tFtkp/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20250508](https://drive.google.com/file/d/17GeetSnT5wW3xNuAHI95-SI1gPGd5sJ_/view) | SAIL Model: [20250709](https://github.com/riscv/sail-riscv/tree/63661df518d18ae71b117245775373b9b21e5a3b) ## Example scenario In the CV32A60X configuration, the first instruction that is decoded is `0x8C7C` at t_id (`t##2`). title: [BUG] SystemVerilog port type compatibility issue: packet_type_o enum port declaration triggers DSim PortTypeMismatch
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

**Summary**

Altair DSim 2026.0 simulator elaboration fails due to a type mismatch on the `rv_tracer.packet_type_o` port connection in `ariane_testharness`.

**Observed Error (DSim)**
```
=E:[PortTypeMismatch]:
  ariane_testharness.sv:727 packet_type_o
  formal: enum logic[3:0]{...}[0:0]
  actual: enum logic[3:0]{...}
```

**Relevant Code**
```
corev_apu/instr_tracing/rv_tracer-main/rtl/rv_tracer.sv(line 60)
corev_apu/instr_tracing/rv_tracer-main/include/te_pkg.sv (line 172)
corev_apu/tb/ariane_testharness.sv (line 727)

```

**Root cause (based on code inspection)**

In `corev_apu/.../rv_tracer.sv` (line 60), the port is declared as an unpacked array of an enum type:

```
output te_pkg::it_packet_type_e [N-1:0] packet_type_o,
```

The instantiation parameter `N` is set to 1, while `te_pkg::it_packet_type_e` (in `te_pkg.sv`) is defined as an enumerated type with packed bit-width `[3:0]`. With `N=1`, the port becomes a single-element unpacked array (`[0:0]`) of a scalar enum, which is not type-compatible with a scalar enum connection under strict SystemVerilog typing. DSim therefore correctly flags this as a fatal type error.

Per Mike Thompson’s suggestion (based on `git blame`), could a maintainer please assign this issue to Jean Roch Coulon?

Thanks.

title: [Bug Report] Incorrect exception type of PMP violation during address translation
body:
Our co-simulation framework found that the exception type of address translation PMP violation is incorrect.

In the following test case, we let a non-leaf (level 2) PTE out of the PMP range.
Next, we will perform a store operation with a special virtual address, during translation processor will try to access the PTE that does not match any PMP.
cva6 throws a load access fault, while spike throws a store access fault.

```
[cva6]  Exception @    119000, PC: 000000008000036c, Cause: Load Access Fault,
[cva6]                                 tval: 0000000080102008
[spike] core   0: 0x000000008000036c (0x00b52023) sw      a1, 0(a0)
[spike] core   0: exception trap_store_access_fault, epc 0x000000008000036c
[spike] core   0:           tval 0x0000000040201010
[spike] core   0: 0x0000000080000004 (0x34302f73) csrr    t5, mtval
[error] WDATA SIM 0000000040201010, DUT 0000000080102008
[error] check board clear 30 error
```

According to riscv-privileged specification:
> If accessing pte violates a PMA or PMP check, raise an access-fault exception corresponding to the original access type.

Hence, cva6 should throw a store access fault.

title: Immediate assertions in the CVA6 RTL
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

This issue is motivated by #1619.

A quick grep of the CVA6 RTL reveals approximately 50 `assert` statements of the form `assert (expression);`. These are called "_immediate assertions_" in the SystemVerilog LRM.  Immediate assertions without an `else` clause are dangerous because they will only emit a simulator-specific message to stdout, without interacting with the simulator or the testbench.  That is, once the assertion fires and the message is written to stdout, there is no further record of the assertion, so it is not possible for the testbench to know that the assertion happened, and bugs can be missed.

For that reason there should be an _else_ clause for all assertions:
```
assert (expression)
  else `uvm_error("<Identifier>", "Useful (?) error message")
```
In non-UVM environments. the `uvm_error()` could be replaced with either $error() or $fatal().  In these cases, the script that launches the simulation must post-process the logfile to check for these messages.  This is not considered ideal since it is easy for the error message in the logfile to be missed.

To resolve this Issue I propose the following:
- Create a "_cvv_error()_" macro that will emit either a `uvm_error()` for UVM simulations or `$fatal()` for non-UVM sims.
- Update all immediate assertions to add an `else` clause as follows:
```
assert(expression)
  else `cvv_error("<Identifier>", "Useful (?) error message")
```

comments.body: @AnouarZajni  I assigned you to this issue because the point need to be discussed. Fix or not fix, that is the question.

Hi @MikeOpenHWGroup,
Yes immediate assertions without else $error/$fatal will printout to stdout but also will change the simulator exit status to "1". Unfortunately cva6.py is not catching any exit status and hence can make the test PASS even with an assert failure.
it's true that using 'else `cvv_error("<Identifier>", "Useful (?) error message")' will solve partially the problem (Different macro for RTL and UVM) but this will generate many file modifications, I will suggest to update cva6.py to catch the exit code instead which will be also useful for any other errors like OS ones.

Regards,
Anouar

> we propose to add an "else" with "$error()"

This is much better.  It still leaves us vulnerable to missing a failed simulation.  The behaviour of `$error()` is not fully specified in the IEEE-1800 specification and so each simulator will behave differently.  Usually, the simulator will print an error message to the logfile.  This is good, but it is very, very easy to miss these and we run the risk of having "false positives".

**_If_** the simulator returns an error code **_and_** we also follow @AnouarZajni's suggestion to update cva6.py to catch the exit code then we should be OK.

Even with this we are exposed.  I recommend creating a macro for the error like this (adopted from [lowRISC Ibex](https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/blob/78739562ce7b2606c4e208d4029ab890255769f6/vendor/lowrisc_ip/ip/prim/rtl/prim_assert.sv#L27)):
```
// Converts an arbitrary block of code into a Verilog string
`define PRIM_STRINGIFY(__x) `"__x`"

// ASSERT_ERROR logs an error message with either `uvm_error or with $error.
//
// This somewhat duplicates `DV_ERROR macro defined in hw/dv/sv/dv_utils/dv_macros.svh. The reason
// for redefining it here is to avoid creating a dependency.
`define ASSERT_ERROR(__name)                                                             \
`ifdef UVM                                                                               \
  uvm_pkg::uvm_report_error("ASSERT FAILED", `PRIM_STRINGIFY(__name), uvm_pkg::UVM_NONE, \
                            `__FILE__, `__LINE__, "", 1);                                \
`else                                                                                    \
  $error("%0t: (%0s:%0d) [%m] [ASSERT FAILED] %0s", $time, `__FILE__, `__LINE__,         \
         `PRIM_STRINGIFY(__name));                                                       \
`endif
```
Then you can have add an "else" with "`ASSERT_ERROR()" and it will work with both UVM and non-UVM testbenches.

Spike code assumes that standard extension bits `MAFDQCHV` of the `Extensions` field in `misa` CSR are writable (see `riscv/csrs.cc:622`).  On the other hand, the privileged spec (Version 20211203, page 16) states that:

> The Extensions field is a WARL field that ***can*** contain

Since in CVA6 the ISA is non-modifiable, the set of writable `misa.Extensions` bits should be reduced to empty using a Spike configuration parameter.

body:

### Bug Description

Hi,

While running a custom Sv39 page-fault test on CVA6, I noticed that the RVFI tracer does not print the cause string for page faults.

Currently, the tracer decodes causes up to store access fault (0x7) and machine ecall (0xb), but it does not include:

- 0xc: Instruction page fault
- 0xd: Load page fault
- 0xf: Store/AMO page fault

As a result, when a page fault occurs, the output looks like:

    exception @ 0x... (0x...)

The RVFI cause value itself is correct (e.g., 0xf for store page fault), but the tracer does not map it to a readable string.

Suggested fix:

Add the missing cases in the tracer:

32'hc: cause = "INSTR_PAGE_FAULT";
32'hd: cause = "LOAD_PAGE_FAULT";
32'hf: cause = "STORE_PAGE_FAULT";

title: Mstatus bug in RISCV CVA6
body:
Hello, @ASintzoff @JeanRochCoulon 
I have been using the RISCV-DV (I use VCS to compile and run the generator), to improve the Code coverage of the CVA6 Core processor, by generating tests from the RISCV-DV using a YAML description, and while trying to access the CVA6’ CSRs, After a failed test, comparing the output of CVA6 with the reference model (spike), I found a mismatch between CVA6 and ref model Spike, the mismatch was in the Mstatus register, is a MXLEN-bit read/write register (64 bits for my case), formatted as shown in Figure 3.7 in (The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual Volume II: Privileged Architecture). The mstatus register keeps track of and controls the hart’s current operating state.
 
The problem appears clearly in WPRI (Some whole read/write fields are reserved for future use. Software should ignore the values read from these fields, and should preserve the values held in these fields when writing values to other fields of the same register. For forward compatibility, implementations that do not furnish these fields must make them read-only zero. These fields are labeled WPRI in the register descriptions) field (Spike read-only zero, while CVA6 read a different value).
In some tests, we found a mismatch also in other fields, for example the UBE field, SPP and SBE.
So to reproduce the problem, I recommend use the RISCV-DV using the YAML description in cva6/dev branch, core-v-verif/cva6/sim/cva6_base_testlist.yaml (https://github.com/openhwgroup/core-v-verif/blob/cva6/dev/cva6/sim/cva6_base_testlist.yaml), adding to this list the description to reproduce the bug:

title: [BUG] Spike version checks in regression scripts are unreliable
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Verification script `verif/sim/cva6.py` performs version consistency checks on several tools including Spike.  For Spike it compares the built-in version string based on the short Git hash (SHA1 checksum) against the short hash of the Spike source.  There are three cases of false negatives in the current implementation of these checks:

1. The short form of the hash has a length that is Git version-dependent. On RedHat Enterprise Linux, the short hash is 9 hex digits long whereas the built-in version string is built by `fprintf`-ing an unsigned integer (32 bits, 8 hex digits) thus causing the most significant digit to be truncated.
2. The "hex number + `fprintf`" approach is not robust against leading zeroes in hash value.
3. The use of "relative level-up" path (`..`) in `git log` invocations used to obtain the hash of the enclosing directory triggers a buggy behavior in Git: even when the `..` is separated from commit-related information using a double dash (`--`), it gets interpreted as a commit-relative expression, yielding highly unexpected results.

**Examples** using openhwgroup/cva6@807ed7825 and openhwgroup/core-v-verif@8e8a63730, openhwgroup/core-v-verif@c98a21182:

- point 1 - note the truncated leading `8` in the actual version string, even though the CFLAGS contain the correct value `-DSPIKE_HASH_VERSION=0x8e8a63730`:
```
$ bash verif/regress/smoke-tests.sh
...
Tue, 14 May 2024 15:15:40 ERROR    You are currently using version 1.1.1-dev e8a63730 of Spike, should be: 1.1.1-dev 8e8a63730. Please install or reinstall it with the installation script.
....
$ tools/spike/bin/spike -v
1.1.1-dev e8a63730
$
```

- point 3 occurs only when the `core-v-verif` commit being used is a merge point (e.g., core-v-verif@c98a21182):
```
$ (cd verif/core-v-verif/vendor/riscv/riscv-isa-sim/build ; git log -1 --pretty=tformat:%h -- ..)
      1 8e8a63730
$ (cd verif/core-v-verif/vendor/riscv/riscv-isa-sim ; git log -1 --pretty=tformat:%h)
      1 8e8a63730
$ (cd verif/core-v-verif ; git checkout c98a21182)
Previous HEAD position was 8e8a63730 Revert "Implementation of Spike param via Yaml files"
HEAD is now at c98a21182 Merge pull request #2419 from ThalesSiliconSecurity/revert
$ (cd verif/core-v-verif/vendor/riscv/riscv-isa-sim/build ; git log -1 --pretty=tformat:%h -- ..)
      1 8e8a63730
$ (cd verif/core-v-verif/vendor/riscv/riscv-isa-sim ; git log -1 --pretty=tformat:%h)
      1 c98a21182
$ 
```

fix_commits.messageHeadline: [Issue #2110] Use actual hash of CVV merge point for Spike version ch…

comments.body: The solution will require a coordinated modification of both repos: `core-v-verif` for Spike build, and `cva6` to remove '`..`' from `git log` invocation.

Fixed in commit [e6c3bac](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/e6c3bac01e4423c828f80b0af324d96f80c4e135) by aligning the behavior of Git hash extraction in Spike build inside `core-v-verif` and in `verif/sim/cva6.py`.  From now on, the project-wide hash of `core-v-verif` is used on both sides.

I was able to run the hello.c program on the Verilator simulator as suggested. Here are the steps I followed: 

Compile the .c file using the following command (you need to have the riscv-tests repo checked-out):
```
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -I./riscv-tests/benchmarks/../env -I./riscv-tests/benchmarks/common \
-DPREALLOCATE=1 -mcmodel=medany -static -std=gnu99 -O2 -ffast-math -fno-common \
-fno-builtin-printf -o hello.riscv hello.c ./riscv-tests/benchmarks/common/syscalls.c \
./riscv-tests/benchmarks/common/crt.S -static -nostdlib -nostartfiles -lm -lgcc \
-T ./riscv-tests/benchmarks/common/test.ld
```
Use the generated ELF file as an input to the Verilator model:
```
obj_dir/Variane_wrapped -p --vcd=dump.vcd hello.riscv
```
